events.description: Congressional act of May 27, 1908 enacted, changing conditions for Five Civilized Tribes regarding land and restrictions
Members of the Five Civilized Tribes contributed financially and with their lives during the great World War
J. R. Phillips began serving under Gabe E. Parker, Superintendent for the Five Civilized Tribes, in 1916
Letter sent from Commissioner of Indian Affairs to superintendents requesting information on releasing Indians from Government supervision
Board of Indian Commissioners Bulletin No. 147 published, containing eight letters on releasing Indians from Government supervision
Board of Indian Commissioners sent letter to Commissioner of Indian Affairs enclosing replies to letters regarding patent-in-fee Indians
Competency commission arbitrarily removed restrictions from certain Indian allottees two or three years before the reports were written (approximately 1918-1919)
Allotment of land in severalty occurred in Creek Nation; prior to allotment Indians held land in common
Tax deeds issued on Indian lands where taxes went unpaid due to inexperience with taxation system
Sales of inherited lands by heirs of deceased allottees revealed 75% or more sold for 50% or less of real value

financial_transactions.description: 75% or more of inherited lands sold by Indian heirs for 50% or less of their real value
Allotments sold far below real value after restrictions removed, proceeds spent unwisely

financial_transactions.amount: fraction of real value, cash in advance for 5 years
financial_transactions.description: At least 90% of allottees leased surplus land for agricultural purposes for five years for cash in advance at only a fraction of real rental value; money soon spent
Purchasers of Indian allotments were able to secure loans from loan companies on the land in excess of the purchase price paid
Inherited lands of deceased allottees sold at price far below real value on approval of county court without Department supervision

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Okmulgee, Oklahoma, Five Civilized Tribes; enrolled member Chickasaw tribe
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision; restriction policy; land sales; education
testimony.key_claims: 30% of Indians under his supervision given freedom from Government control are making decided success; 50% succeeding indifferently well; 10% barely escape failure; 10% have failed completely. Competent Indians rarely apply for removal of restrictions because restricted land is non-taxable and they value their homes. 10% of those whose restrictions were removed by competency commission have sold their lands and misused proceeds; 90% have made good. Full-blood Indians enrolled as less than full-blood due to enrollment irregularities. Education is the only solution. Opposes both total removal of restrictions and keeping all restricted. Supports middle course. Proposes Secretary of Interior approval for conveyance of deceased allottees' lands. Members of Five Civilized Tribes served in World War I financially and with lives.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Holdenville, Oklahoma, Five Civilized Tribes
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision; restriction removal; inherited lands; taxation; guardianship; leasing
testimony.key_claims: Very small percentage of fully released Indians in his district are making a success. At least 75% of those whose restrictions removed have disposed of their allotments. When restriction removal order becomes effective, Indians proceed to sell land or encumber it with loans. Purchasers secure loans from loan companies in excess of purchase price. Indians inexperienced with taxes leave them unpaid; penalties accrue; tax deeds issued. At least 90% of allottees lease surplus land for cash in advance at fraction of real value; money soon spent; allottee left without support, becomes idler. Inherited lands revealed upon examination to be 75% or more sold for 50% or less of real value. Probate court sales inadequately supervised; US probate attorneys' protests ignored. Proposes legislation requiring appraisal and advertisement for inherited land sales, impounding proceeds. Proposes Congress require all lease contracts under field clerk supervision. Proposes compulsory retention of 40 acres homestead.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Ardmore, Oklahoma, Five Civilized Tribes
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy; merit-based restriction removal; reservation of homestead land
testimony.key_claims: Policy of granting patents-in-fee has been premature in many cases; trust created by Congress has not been kept as intended; injury rather than good has resulted. Matter of removal of restrictions should be decided on merits not quantum of Indian blood. Many less-than-half-bloods less fit than full-bloods. Too much liberality in general removal of restrictions from less-than-half-bloods has made them prey of designing, resourceful men. Would reserve 40 acres of average land restricted until death as homestead, also becoming heritage to heirs born after tribal rolls closed. Believes much damage has been done that would have been avoided with earlier action. In his opinion only small percent have made full success after restriction removal; majority not going forward as hoped.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Crow Indian Reservation, Crow Agency, Montana
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Crow Indians from Government supervision; patent-in-fee conditions
testimony.key_claims: Compiled tabular statement showing data on patent-in-fee Indians. Has little to add to letters from field matron and farmers, especially missionary whose views align closely with his own. Wrote to all farmers, field matrons, and missionaries after receiving March 31, 1921 circular. Had hoped for report from Father Taelman who worked among Indians long time but not received. Believes individual allotments should be given with responsibility forced upon Indians, not nurtured; younger people with schooling should receive their portion and learn consequences of indolence.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Letter described by Asbury as not sentimental but cold-blooded; views nearly identical to Asbury's own opinion. Has charge of extensive missionary work including community and school activities. Believes Indians must be put on their own responsibility and this cannot be achieved through nursing but must be forced upon them.
